title: Sales Commission Capitalization Under ASC 340-40: A SaaS Guide
summary: Sales commission capitalization under ASC 340-40, explained for SaaS. See which commissions to capitalize and how to set the amortization period.
body_markdown:
## What Is Sales Commission Capitalization?


Sales commission capitalization records the commission that won a contract as a balance sheet asset under ASC 340-40-25-1, then amortizes it over the benefit period. The subtopic is ASC 340-40, Other Assets and Deferred Costs, Contracts with Customers, created alongside Topic 606 by[ASU 2014-09](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202014-09_Section%20A.pdf) .


Capitalization is not an election.


Four mechanics decide how the account behaves:


- **Two branches, one caption.** Costs to obtain a contract sit at ASC 340-40-25-1 through 25-4. Costs to fulfill sit at 25-5 through 25-8. Commissions live in the first branch, implementation and migration labor in the second, and the two are tested against different criteria. A single deferred contract costs account with no sub-ledger behind it is an audit finding waiting to happen.
- **Recognition is mandatory.** PwC’s contract cost guidance states that expensing these costs as incurred isn’t permitted unless they qualify for the practical expedient.
- **Two tests, both required.** ASC 340-40-25-1 imposes an incremental test and a recoverability test. Recoverability can be assessed contract by contract or on a portfolio basis, using expected consideration from the contract plus anticipated renewals.
- **It isn’t a contract asset.** The capitalized commission is a separate deferred cost, split current and noncurrent, not the contract asset defined in ASC 606-10-45-1.[CrowdStrike’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended April 30, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1535527/000153552725000019/crwd-20250430.htm) shows the shape a diligence team looks for first, $351.8 million current and $496.0 million noncurrent.


Private companies have no exit here. Topic 606 and Subtopic 340-40 took effect for private entities for annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2019 following the deferral in ASU 2020-05, and there’s no scope exception and no small-company carve-out for contract costs. A private SaaS company issuing GAAP financials in 2026 has been in scope for six full reporting years. This page owns the cost side of the contract. The revenue side is covered in[ASC 606](https://www.indinero.com/blog/asc-606-what-you-need-to-know/) , and the liability mechanics in[deferred revenue tax treatment](https://www.indinero.com/blog/deferred-revenue-tax-treatment/) .


## The ASC 340-40 Contract Cost Model


The ASC 340-40 contract cost model runs three tests in sequence: incremental under 25-2, amortization period under 35-1, then the 25-4 expedient. Get the first one wrong and the other two don’t matter.


The order also tells you where to spend review time. The incremental test is answered by a document you already have, the current commission plan. The amortization period is an accounting estimate you have to build, support, and refresh annually. The expedient is a policy election that SaaS companies routinely claim more broadly than the standard allows.


Grant Thornton’s guide to[navigating ASC 606 and 340-40](https://www.grantthornton.com/content/dam/grantthornton/website/assets/content-page-files/audit/pdfs/2026/revenue-from-contracts-with-customers-navigating-the-guidance-in-asc-606-and-340-40-revised-april-2026.pdf) treats the two subtopics as a single workstream, which is the right instinct. The capitalize-versus-expense discipline is the same one you apply to[capital expenditures](https://www.indinero.com/blog/small-business-capex/) , except the useful life is a customer relationship rather than a machine, and you estimate it from churn data instead of reading it off a depreciation table.


### Incremental Costs of Obtaining a Contract


ASC 340-40-25-2 defines incremental costs of obtaining a contract as costs the entity wouldn’t have incurred if the contract hadn’t been obtained. The working test is a counterfactual. Would you have paid this if the customer had walked away the minute before signature.


Compensation element Capitalize? Authority


AE commission paid only on closed-won Yes ASC 340-40-25-2


Sales manager or regional override on the same deal Yes. Title and org level aren’t determining factors FASB Implementation Q&A 78


Tiered commission (0% on deals 1 to 9, 5% at 20+) Yes. The payment wouldn’t have occurred absent the contracts FASB Implementation Q&A 78


Payroll taxes and 401(k) match on the capitalized commission Yes, where the amount is driven by the commission Deloitte Roadmap 13.2


Channel referral fee contingent on a signed contract Yes CrowdStrike disclosed policy


Fixed AE base salary No. Incurred regardless of contract volume ASC 340-40-25-3


Discretionary bonus on growth, profitability, and performance No. Not attributable to identifiable contracts FASB Implementation Q&A 78


Bid, proposal, legal, and travel costs on a lost deal No ASC 340-40-25-3


Two edge cases decide most disputes. ASC 340-40-25-3 expenses costs incurred regardless of outcome unless they’re explicitly chargeable to the customer either way, in which case they’re receivables, not contract costs. And a commission that requires continued employment or continued service after signature isn’t incremental to obtaining the contract, a point[Deloitte’s revenue roadmap](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/codification/revenue/asc606-10/roadmap-revenue-recognition/chapter-13-contract-costs/13-2-costs-obtaining-a-contract) routes through ASC 710 first. A clawback that lapses over 12 months of employment is exactly that fact pattern, and it’s one of the most common SaaS plan designs in the market.


[FASB Implementation Q&A 78](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/fasb_financial_accou/trg_revenue/trg_revenue_US/revenue-recognition-implementation-q-as/CONTRACT_COSTS_75/Question_78_90.html) settles the override and threshold questions in plain language. What most teams miss is procedural. This determination isn’t made in the general ledger, it’s made in the plan document, and a single mid-year amendment changes the accounting for every deal booked after the effective date. The offsetting credit sits in[accrued commissions payable](https://www.indinero.com/blog/accrued-expenses-simple/) until payroll runs, which is where the tie-out to cash begins.


### Choosing the Amortization Period


ASC 340-40-35-1 requires amortization on a systematic basis consistent with the transfer of the goods or services the asset relates to. The same paragraph contemplates an asset relating to services transferred under an anticipated contract the entity can specifically identify. That clause is why SaaS amortization periods routinely run four to seven years against a one-year contract.


The commensurate test is the fork in the road.[FASB Implementation Q&A 71](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/fasb_financial_accou/trg_revenue/trg_revenue_US/revenue-recognition-implementation-q-as/CONTRACT_COSTS_75/Question_71_83.html) and the November 2016 TRG discussion resolve it two ways. If the renewal commission is commensurate, meaning reasonably proportional to the respective contract values, the initial commission amortizes over the initial term and each renewal over its own term. If it isn’t, the asset relates to the anticipated renewals too, and the commission amortization period extends across the expected customer relationship.


Don’t argue the memo on level of effort. The FASB staff rejected that view outright, on the reasoning that effort is about the past while the amortization period is about future transfer of services. Compare rates as a percentage of respective contract value instead.


Company Disclosed period of benefit


CrowdStrike Four years for initial and upsell commissions, renewals over the contractual renewal term


Sprout Social Five years, increased from three years effective January 1, 2024


eGain Five years, supported by an approximately 90% post-initial retention rate


Gartner One year, because renewal commissions equal initial commissions


Gartner and eGain reached opposite conclusions in the same year under the same standard, and the only variable was proportionality. Support your own number with gross logo retention by cohort tied to the billing system, the implied life from annual churn (1 divided by the churn rate), and the technology life cycle argument that caps the period below that math. Segment self-serve and enterprise cohorts separately. Changes are prospective under ASC 340-40-35-2 and ASC 250-10-45-17, and they move real money. Sprout Social’s extension from three years to five reduced sales and marketing expense by $3.4 million for the quarter and $11.5 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2024, per its[Q3 2024 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1517375/000151737524000133/spt-20240930.htm) .


### The One-Year Practical Expedient


ASC 340-40-25-4 lets you expense commissions as incurred only when the amortization period of the asset would be one year or less. The test is the amortization period, not the contract term, and that distinction is where most SaaS companies misapply it.


[PwC’s guidance on incremental costs](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/revenue_from_contrac/revenue_from_contrac_US/chapter_11_contract__US/112incremental_costs_US.html) is explicit that anticipated renewals, amendments, and follow-on contracts with the same customer must be considered when assessing whether the period of benefit is one year or less. A 12-month subscription a customer renews three times has a benefit period well past twelve months. The initial term is irrelevant to the test.


It’s also a policy election, not a per-deal choice. The expedient has to be applied consistently to contracts with similar characteristics, so the memo needs to name the population it covers.


Where it legitimately works in SaaS: annual renewal commissions that are commensurate with the initial commission and amortize inside twelve months, plus month-to-month and self-serve tiers with genuinely short benefit periods.[Gartner’s SEC correspondence](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/749251/000074925120000002/filename1.htm) is the documented public example of a company concluding a one-year period across its whole population. Where it doesn’t work: new logo commissions at a company with 85% or better gross logo retention. The math can’t reach a one-year benefit period, and SEC staff have asked registrants directly whether renewal commissions are commensurate with initial ones. That conclusion belongs in the same[GAAP policy file](https://www.indinero.com/blog/gaap-what-it-is-why-your-investors-expect-it/) as everything else.


## SaaS-Specific Application


ASC 340-40 wasn’t written for subscription models, and SaaS contracts activate every judgment in it, from the 25-2 incremental test to 35-3 impairment. Work a real deal through the ledger and the mechanics stop being abstract.


**The facts.** A B2B SaaS company signs a 36-month subscription on January 1, 2026. Total contract value is $180,000, billed annually, with first-year ACV of $60,000. The plan pays the AE 10% of first-year ACV ($6,000) and the sales manager a 2% override ($1,200). Payroll taxes and 401(k) match on those commissions add $600. The SDR earns $500 per qualified meeting booked whether or not the deal closes, so that fails the counterfactual and is expensed under ASC 340-40-25-3. The AE’s quarterly bonus keys off team quota, net retention, and individual performance, so it isn’t incremental either. Total capitalized: $7,800.


**The period.** Renewals pay 2% against 10% on the initial, so they aren’t commensurate. Gross annual logo churn on the enterprise cohort is 12%, implying a mathematical life of 8.3 years. Management caps the period at 60 months on the strength of a three-year platform technology life cycle and three cohorts of retention data, then documents the cap in the contract cost memo. Straight-line fits, because the obligation is stand-ready and satisfied ratably. Monthly amortization is $7,800 divided by 60, or $130.00.


**The entries.** At booking in January 2026, Dr Deferred contract acquisition costs $7,800, Cr Accrued commissions payable $7,800. Each month for 60 months, Dr Sales and marketing expense (commission amortization) $130, Cr Deferred contract acquisition costs $130. At December 31, 2026, cumulative amortization is $1,560 and the carrying amount is $6,240, classified $1,560 current and $4,680 noncurrent.


**The contrast.** Had the plan paid 10% on renewals, the period would be the 36-month initial term and monthly amortization would be $216.67. Same cash, same plan economics, materially different expense curve. That’s the entire commercial consequence of the commensurate test.


**The impairment.** The customer doesn’t renew at December 31, 2028, leaving a carrying amount of $3,120. ASC 340-40-35-3 writes the asset down to the extent carrying amount exceeds remaining expected consideration less the direct costs of delivering what’s left, and remaining consideration here is zero. Dr Impairment of deferred contract acquisition costs $3,120, Cr Deferred contract acquisition costs $3,120. ASC 340-40-35-6 prohibits reversal. If the logo comes back in 2029, that’s a new contract and a new asset.


Three subscription-specific judgments sit on top of that base case:


- **Ramped contracts.** Amortization follows the transfer of services, not the billing schedule. A contract that ramps $40k, $60k, $80k still amortizes straight-line if the obligation is a single stand-ready promise.
- **Upsell versus renewal.** CrowdStrike’s disclosed policy amortizes initial and upsell commissions over the same four-year benefit period, while renewals follow the contractual renewal term. A mid-term seat expansion is usually a modification under ASC 606-10-25-10 through 25-13, and the commission follows that analysis.
- **Impairment cadence.** ASC 340-40-35-3 has no periodicity limit, and ASC 340-40-35-5 sets the ordering, other guidance first, then contract costs, then the asset group. That means a monthly churn feed from the CRM into the sub-ledger, not an annual sweep.


The failure point is operational, not technical. The capitalized commissions SaaS companies carry need a sub-ledger keyed at the contract line level, not the rep or the pay period, carrying contract ID, booking date, capitalize or expense flag, rationale code, amortization period, cumulative amortization, carrying amount, and impairment history. Add a monthly tie-out to the GL, a reconciliation of the accrual to plan and payroll, and a rate table versioned by plan effective date. Purpose-built commission engines produce the calculation. None of them produce the memo, the incremental determination, or the reconciliation, which is why the[system selection question](https://www.indinero.com/blog/startup-erp-systems/) sits downstream of the policy question.


Two adjacent workstreams deserve a flag. Companies moving off cash-basis books rebuild the asset retrospectively, contract by contract, across every open period, which is a scoped piece of a[cash to accrual conversion](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cash-to-accrual-conversion-saas-playbook/) and belongs on the[GAAP switch checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/gaap-accounting-switch-checklist/) . The asset also creates a book-to-tax difference. Employee compensation is generally treated as not facilitating creation of an intangible under[Treas. Reg. section 1.263(a)-4(e)(4)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.263(a)-4) , so employee commissions are generally deductible currently once the all-events test and economic performance are met. The result is a deferred tax liability growing in step with the asset and a Schedule M adjustment built from the same sub-ledger. That item goes missing when accounting and tax sit at different firms, which is part of why indinero delivers both inside one[SaaS accounting engagement](https://www.indinero.com/industries/saas-accounting-services/) .


## Common Pitfalls


Most contract cost findings under ASC 340-40 are documentation failures rather than technical errors, and the ASC 340-40-50 disclosures are the most commonly missed.


1. **Expensing everything and calling it immaterial with no memo.** This can be a defensible conclusion. It’s never a defensible undocumented one.[SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99](https://www.sec.gov/interps/account/sab99.htm) is the framework auditors reach for, and it’s explicit that a percentage threshold is only the beginning of a materiality analysis.
2. **Using the contract term when renewals pay less.** A 10% new-logo rate against a 2% renewal rate isn’t commensurate, so amortizing over the 12- or 36-month term front-loads expense and understates the asset. This is the exact question SEC staff have put to registrants.
3. **Capitalizing costs that aren’t incremental.** SDR pay earned on meetings booked, base salaries, allocated sales overhead, and multi-factor discretionary bonuses all fail ASC 340-40-25-2. The correction hurts, because the sub-ledger usually has no rationale field to filter on.
4. **Failing to capitalize the manager override.** The mirror-image error, driven by a belief that only the closing rep counts. Title and organizational level aren’t determining factors.
5. **Forgetting to impair when a customer churns.** A five-year period on a customer that terminated in month 14 carries a fictional asset. ASC 340-40-35-3 requires the write-down and there’s no grace period.
6. **Never reconciling the asset to the commission plan.** The control failure that produces every other item on this list. The GL drifts from the sub-ledger, the sub-ledger drifts from the plan, and nobody notices until an auditor pulls a sample.
7. **Missing the ASC 340-40-50 disclosures.** ASC 340-40-50-1 through 50-3 require closing balances by category, amortization and impairment for the period, the judgments made, and the method used to set the period. A footnote saying only that the company capitalizes sales commissions fails all four.
8. **Ignoring the costs-to-fulfill branch.** Implementation and data migration labor can meet ASC 340-40-25-5, while ASC 340-40-25-8 still expenses general and administrative costs, unproductive labor, and learning-curve inefficiency immediately.


Items 1, 6, and 7 are process problems a bookkeeping-only provider never surfaces, because booking the cash is the whole job. Indinero’s CPA team catches these during monthly close review, so the memo exists before the auditor asks rather than after. That gap matters more here than elsewhere, since the underlying[accrual mechanics](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cash-vs-accrual/) are straightforward and the documentation around them is what actually fails.


## The Audit-Ready Standard


An auditor can’t test a contract cost asset without three artifacts: the ASC 340-40-25 policy memo, the contract-level sub-ledger, and its monthly reconciliation. Build all three at adoption, not the week fieldwork starts.


The package that survives a first-time audit or a Series B diligence request:


- **The contract cost policy memo.** Names the population, states the incremental determination for every element of every active plan version, states the recoverability conclusion and whether it’s contract or portfolio level, states whether the ASC 340-40-25-4 expedient is elected and over which population, and states the amortization method.
- **The amortization period memo, refreshed annually.** This is the estimate the auditor focuses on under[PCAOB AS 2501](https://pcaobus.org/oversight/standards/auditing-standards/details/AS2501) , which directs attention to estimates with greater risk of material misstatement and to evidence of management bias. It needs the commensurate analysis as rates against respective contract values, cohort retention data with a source tie, the implied life calculation, the capping factors, and a stated conclusion.
- **The sub-ledger and its reconciliation.** Opening balance, additions, amortization, impairments, closing balance, tied to the GL and signed off monthly.
- **Commission plan documents for every version, with effective dates.** The primary evidence behind every incremental call.
- **The churn and impairment log.** Open balances flagged against a churn feed, with write-offs traceable to the termination date.
- **The disclosures and the book-to-tax bridge.** The ASC 340-40-50 items, plus the deferred tax computation drawn from the same sub-ledger.


The plan document is the audit trail.


Indinero’s books are audit-ready by default, because GAAP discipline is baked into how the team operates, not added later. That package isn’t assembled for the audit. It exists because the close produced it, which is the practical difference between[audit preparation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/audit-preparation/) as a data pull and audit preparation as a six-week reconstruction. The same standard runs through the rest of[GAAP accounting for startups](https://www.indinero.com/blog/gaap-accounting-for-startups/) .

## Frequently asked questions


The questions Controllers and VPs of Finance ask most often about capitalizing sales commissions under ASC 340-40, answered below.


### Does a private SaaS company have to capitalize sales commissions?


Yes, ASC 340-40 applies to private SaaS companies with no scope exception and no small entity carve-out for capitalizing sales commissions. Topic 606 and Subtopic 340-40 took effect for private entities for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2019. The only routes to expensing are the ASC 340-40-25-4 practical expedient or a documented materiality conclusion, and indinero’s CPA team writes that memo inside the monthly close, before a diligence request forces it.


### How do you set the amortization period when customers renew?


Set the amortization period by comparing the renewal commission rate to the initial rate, each as a percentage of respective contract value. If the rates are reasonably proportional, the commission is commensurate under FASB Implementation Q&A 71 and amortizes over the initial term, with each renewal over its own term. If renewals pay materially less, ASC 340-40-35-1 extends the period across the expected customer relationship, supported by cohort retention data and a technology life cycle cap.


### Are SDR commissions and sales manager overrides capitalizable?


Sales manager overrides on a closed-won deal are capitalizable, while SDR pay earned per meeting booked is not. FASB Implementation Q&A 78 states that an employee’s title or level in the organization isn’t a determining factor, so the override follows the same treatment as the rep’s commission. Meeting-based SDR pay fails the ASC 340-40-25-2 counterfactual and is expensed under ASC 340-40-25-3, though an SDR fee paid only on a closed-won deal passes, as do payroll taxes computed on capitalized commissions.


### What happens to the capitalized asset when a customer churns early?


A capitalized commission asset is impaired when a customer churns early, and ASC 340-40-35-6 prohibits reversing that write-down later. ASC 340-40-35-3 recognizes the loss to the extent carrying amount exceeds the remaining consideration expected, less the direct costs of delivering what’s left, and a termination usually drives that consideration to zero. Catching it on time takes a monthly churn feed into the commission sub-ledger, which indinero runs as a close step rather than an annual sweep.


### Can we expense commissions if every contract is 12 months?


Usually not, because the ASC 340-40-25-4 practical expedient tests the commission’s amortization period, not the 12-month contract term. Anticipated renewals, amendments, and follow-on contracts with the same customer count toward the period of benefit, so a company with 85% or better gross logo retention can’t reach one year on new logo commissions. The expedient is a policy election applied consistently to contracts with similar characteristics, so name the population it covers in the memo.
